The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix an integer $N\ge2$. Write $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ for the complex $N\times N$ matrices, $U^*=\overline U^{\mathsf T}$ for conjugate transpose, and $I_N$ for the identity matrix. Define the special unitary matrix group

$$SU(N):=\{U\in\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_N,\ \det U=1\},$$

with matrix multiplication and the following real embedded smooth structure. Identify $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ with $\mathbb R^{2N^2}$ by the real and imaginary matrix entries, and let $\operatorname{Herm}_N=\{H:H^*=H\}$ have its induced real vector-space structure. Equip $U(N)=\{U:U^*U=I_N\}$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $I_N$ of the smooth map $F:\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)\to\operatorname{Herm}_N$, $F(U)=U^*U$, where $\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)=\{U:\det U\ne0\}$. Equip $S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ with its embedded circle structure and $SU(N)$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $1$ of $\det:U(N)\to S^1$. These are the embedded structures in the stated real matrix space. Its real Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{su}(N):=\{X\in\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C):X^*=-X,\ \operatorname{tr}X=0\}$ with bracket $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. The standard unitary representation is the map $\rho:SU(N)\to U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ defined by $\rho(U)v=Uv$, where $h(v,w)=\sum_{j=1}^N\overline{v_j}w_j$ and $U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ consists of the complex-linear maps preserving $h$. Conjugation is $\operatorname{Ad}_U z=UzU^{-1}$ for either $z\in SU(N)$ or $z\in\mathfrak{su}(N)$.

Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the representation $\rho$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.

Choose one finite smooth bundle atlas of local sections $(U_\alpha,s_\alpha)$ whose coordinate images are bounded balls, and a subordinate partition of unity with each cutoff compactly supported in its chart. On an overlap write $s_\beta=s_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$ for its smooth transition map $g_{\alpha\beta}:U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\to SU(N)$. Local representatives of an adjoint section $\xi$ and an adjoint group section $u$ are defined by $\xi(x)=[s_\alpha(x),\xi_\alpha(x)]$ and $u(x)=[s_\alpha(x),u_\alpha(x)]$. They obey the transition rules $\xi_\beta=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}}\xi_\alpha$ and $u_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}u_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$.

For each integer $k>d/2+1$, define $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ by completion of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms, using weak derivatives of their local coefficients. Define $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ as the corresponding completion of smooth group-bundle sections, represented locally by matrix-valued $H^{k+1}$ maps satisfying the stated transition rule. After localization by the partition of unity and extension by zero to the coordinate balls, the higher-order Sobolev embedding gives unique continuous representatives (indeed $C^1$); the group-valued representatives take values in the closed subgroup $SU(N)$ everywhere. This embedding is the point-evaluation convention used below. If $p\in P$ lies over $x$ and $p=s_\alpha(x)h$, define $u(p):=h^{-1}u_\alpha(x)h$. The transition rule makes this independent of the chosen local section, and $u(x)=[p,u(p)]$. In particular, if $p_m=s_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$, then $u(p_m)=h_{\alpha m}^{-1}u_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$ is the value in the $p_m$-trivialization. The map $\widetilde u:P\to P$ defined by $\widetilde u(p):=p\,u(p)$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$, with inverse $\widetilde{u^{-1}}$; it is smooth when $u$ is smooth. Conversely, if $\Phi:P\to P$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$ commuting with the right $SU(N)$ action, write $\Phi(p)=p\,g_p$ for the unique $g_p\in SU(N)$. Equivariance gives $g_{ph}=h^{-1}g_ph$, so $u(x):=[p,g_p]$ for $p\in P_x$ is a well-defined $C^1$ adjoint-group section. These assignments are inverse; in the smooth case they identify smooth sections with the smooth gauge group defined by principal-bundle automorphisms.

Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$, equivalently the sections whose associated bundle automorphism fixes $p_m$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology and multiplication $[u][v]=[uv]$, well-defined since $Z_N$ is central.

Specify its Hilbert Lie structure as follows, using the Hilbert Lie structure on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ established by the calculus lemma. Let $q:\mathcal G_{k+1}\to\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ be the coset projection. Since $Z_N$ is finite and the group is Hausdorff, choose an identity chart neighborhood $V$ with $V^{-1}V\cap Z_N=\{e\}$, by continuity of $(v,w)\mapsto v^{-1}w$ at $(e,e)$. The map $q$ is open because $q^{-1}(q(O))=\bigcup_{z\in Z_N}Oz$ for every open $O$. Consequently $q|_{uV}:uV\to q(uV)$ is a homeomorphism for each $u$, and transport the translated Hilbert charts through these maps. On an overlap, two lifts differ locally by multiplication by a fixed element of the discrete group $Z_N$, so chart changes are smooth. Distinct cosets have disjoint open neighborhoods: if $v^{-1}w\notin Z_N$, continuity and finiteness give neighborhoods $O_v,O_w$ with $O_v^{-1}O_w\cap Z_N=\varnothing$, and their images under $q$ are disjoint. Thus the quotient is Hausdorff. Its countable base descends from that of the Sobolev section space by the open map $q$. Multiplication and inversion are smooth in these charts because they lift locally to the corresponding smooth operations on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. This defines a Hilbert Lie group with the stated quotient topology, and $q$ is a local diffeomorphism.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty:=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ be the group of smooth adjoint-group sections under pointwise multiplication, identified above with the smooth gauge group. Give it the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. For a connection form $\omega$, write $A_\alpha=s_\alpha^*\omega$ for its local form. The right-principal convention gives $A_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}A_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$. The right gauge action is locally $A_\alpha^u:=u_\alpha^{-1}A_\alpha u_\alpha+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha$. For smooth $u$, this is the pullback by $\widetilde u$: for $X\in T_xM$, $d(\widetilde u\circ s_\alpha)_xX=d(R_{u_\alpha(x)})_{s_\alpha(x)}\,ds_\alpha(X)+(u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha(X))_P(s_\alpha(x)u_\alpha(x))$, and the connection equivariance and vertical reproduction identities give the displayed formula. For Sobolev $u$, the calculus lemma verifies that the local forms patch under the stated transition rules and define a smooth action on the Sobolev spaces above. For an adjoint section $\xi$, set $d_A\xi:=d\xi+[A,\xi]$ using the degree-one Lie-algebra-valued-form bracket. In local coordinates and an orthonormal adjoint frame, define the formal adjoint on an adjoint-valued one-form $a$ by $(d_A^*a)=-g^{ij}(\nabla_i^{\mathrm{LC}}a_j+[A_i,a_j])$, where $\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}$ differentiates the covector index. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

For $A\in\mathcal A_k$, parallel transport of its $C^1$ connection form around piecewise smooth loops based at $p_m$ defines a subgroup $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)\subseteq SU(N)$. Call $A$ irreducible when this subgroup leaves no nonzero proper complex subspace of $\mathbb C^N$ invariant; changing the chosen frame conjugates the subgroup and leaves this condition unchanged. Write $\mathcal A_k^*$ and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ for the irreducible loci. Once the calculus lemma verifies the group action, define orbit equivalence by $A\sim B$ exactly when $B=A^u$ for some gauge section $u$; all resulting quotients carry the quotient topology, whose open sets are those with open inverse image under the orbit projection.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$, $Y$ be real
Banach spaces, let $U \subseteq X$ be open, let $f : U \to Y$ be of class $C^k$
with $k \ge 1$ ([[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]]), and let $a \in U$. If
$Df(a) : X \to Y$ is a bounded linear isomorphism — that is, $Df(a)$ is
bijective and its inverse $Df(a)^{-1} : Y \to X$ is bounded — then there are
open sets $U_0 \subseteq U$ with $a \in U_0$ and $V_0 \subseteq Y$ with
$f(a) \in V_0$ such that $f|_{U_0} : U_0 \to V_0$ is a bijection and its inverse
$g := (f|_{U_0})^{-1} : V_0 \to U_0$ is of class $C^k$, with

$$Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr) = Df(x)^{-1} \qquad \text{for every } x \in U_0 .$$

derivations.claim: On an overlap of two relatively compact bundle charts, a localized section changes coordinates by multiplication by a smooth transition matrix and by a smooth coordinate change. Every derivative of order at most $k$ of the transformed coefficient is a finite sum of bounded derivatives of these transition maps times derivatives of the original coefficient of order at most $k$. The Jacobians and inverse Jacobians are bounded on the compact supports. The product and chain rules therefore bound each localized $H^k$ norm by a constant times the finite-atlas norm in the other chart. Summing over the finite cover gives both norm inequalities. Thus the norms are equivalent and define the same complete Sobolev topology.

Localize by the fixed finite partition and extend each compactly supported coefficient by zero into a bounded Euclidean ball. For $p=2$, $2k>d$; [F2] gives the scalar $H^k$ product estimate and the $C^1$ representative when $k>d/2+1$. To estimate a localized product, multiply one factor by the partition cutoff and the other by an auxiliary smooth cutoff equal to one on its support. Summing the finitely many coefficient estimates gives bounded matrix multiplication on $H^k(\mathcal M)$; conjugation preserves products, so they patch. The commutator of two anti-Hermitian trace-zero matrices is anti-Hermitian and trace-zero, giving the stated adjoint-bundle bracket bound. Matrix multiplication itself need not preserve $\operatorname{ad}P$. The same reasoning at order $k+1$ gives its matrix-section algebra estimate and continuous embedding. The completed vector-section spaces are Hilbert spaces: the sum of the localized $L^2$ derivative inner products induces the chosen norm, and completion preserves that inner product.

Regard $E:=H^{k+1}(\mathcal M)$ as a real Banach algebra with identity section $I_N$ and an equivalent submultiplicative norm, using step 2.1. The map $f:E\to E$, $f(X)=\exp X-I_N$, is $C^\infty$: its power series and all derivatives converge uniformly on bounded balls by the factorial bounds for powers in a Banach algebra. Its derivative at $0$ is $Df(0)=\operatorname{id}_E$. Thus [F3] applies to this map on the open Banach-space domain $E$, giving open neighborhoods $U$ of $0$ and $W$ of $0$ such that $f:U\to W$ is a smooth diffeomorphism. Shrink these neighborhoods so its inverse is the convergent series $\log(I_N+Y)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j+1}Y^j/j$ for $Y\in W$, smooth by locally uniform convergence of its differentiated series. The two series are inverse there, since their absolutely convergent compositions are the scalar formal identities in the single commuting variable $X$ or $Y$.

The real subspace $H:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)\subset E$ is the closed range of the bounded projection $X\mapsto (X-X^*)/2-\operatorname{tr}(X-X^*)I_N/(2N)$: projecting smooth matrix-section approximants proves equality with the completed adjoint section space. Shrink $U$ using the continuous $C^0$ embedding so that $|\operatorname{tr}X(x)|<2\pi$ for every $X\in U$ and $x\in M$, and so that the following logarithm identities hold in their convergence neighborhoods. For $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}\cap(I_N+W)$, the series give $(\log u)^*=\log(u^*)=\log(u^{-1})=-\log u$; the last equality follows from $\exp(-X)=(\exp X)^{-1}$ and the local inverse identities. For any matrix $X$, differentiating the determinant by column multilinearity gives $\frac{d}{dt}\det(e^{tX})=\operatorname{tr}(X)\det(e^{tX})$, hence $\det(e^X)=e^{\operatorname{tr}X}$. Thus $\det u=1$ implies $\operatorname{tr}\log u\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$; the strict trace bound forces it to be zero, so $\log u\in H$. Conjugation commutes with both series, so these assertions patch. Conversely, if $X\in U\cap H$, then $\exp X$ is unitary by $\exp(X)^*=\exp(-X)$ and has determinant one by the same identity. It lies in the defining completion of smooth gauge sections because smooth adjoint sections approximate $X$ and their exponentials converge in $E$. Consequently $\exp$ restricts to a homeomorphism from the open subset $U\cap H$ of $H$ onto the relatively open identity neighborhood $\mathcal G_{k+1}\cap(I_N+W)$, with inverse the restricted smooth logarithm. Here, after each shrinking, take $W=f(U)$; it remains open by step 3.1.

Products and inverses preserve the completion defining $\mathcal G_{k+1}$: multiply smooth approximating gauge sections and use the algebra estimate; for inversion use $u^{-1}=u^*$, a bounded real-linear operation on $E$. Translated charts $u\exp X$ from step 4.1 cover the group and induce its given Sobolev topology, since translation and its inverse are continuous. Their coordinate changes are $X\mapsto\log(v^{-1}u\exp X)$ on the open overlap domains and are smooth by the ambient algebra estimates and series. In coordinates near any $u,v$, multiplication is represented by $\log((uv)^{-1}u\exp X\,v\exp Y)$, and inversion by $\log(u(u\exp X)^{-1})$, wherever these products lie in the identity chart. These expressions are smooth as maps into $E$ and take values in $H$; the subspace norm makes all their derivatives $H$-valued, so they are smooth as maps into $H$. This proves the Hilbert Lie group assertion without treating $SU(N)$-valued sections as an open subset of $E$.

On an overlap, write $s_\beta=s_\alpha g$; the connection and section transition rules are $A_\beta=g^{-1}A_\alpha g+g^{-1}dg$ and $u_\beta=g^{-1}u_\alpha g$. The product rule gives
$$A_\beta^{u_\beta}=g^{-1}\bigl(u_\alpha^{-1}A_\alpha u_\alpha+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha\bigr)g+g^{-1}dg,$$
so the local formula for $A^u$ has exactly the connection transition rule and patches to the pullback by the $C^1$ bundle automorphism associated with $u$. In each chart the action is $A^u=u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$. Multiplication $H^{k+1}\times H^k\to H^k$ is bounded because $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ continuously and the matrix-section $H^k$ product is bounded by step 2.1. Differentiation $H^{k+1}\to H^k$ is bounded and $u^{-1}=u^*$ on the gauge group. Thus both terms are restrictions of compositions of bounded linear and bilinear maps on the local matrix Sobolev spaces, and are smooth in the charts of step 5.1. They have connection-valued output: conjugation preserves $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, while differentiating $u^*u=I_N$ and $\det u=1$ shows $u^{-1}du$ is anti-Hermitian and trace-zero. The composition identity $(A^u)^v=A^{uv}$ follows from $d(uv)=(du)v+u\,dv$, and $A^e=A$, so this is the stated smooth right action.

For $t\in\mathbb R$, expand in the finite-dimensional matrix algebra: $e^{-t\xi}(A+ta)e^{t\xi}=A+t(a+[A,\xi])+o(t)$ in $H^k$, while $e^{-t\xi}d(e^{t\xi})=t\,d\xi+o(t)$ in $H^k$ by the bounded derivative and product estimates of step 2.1. Adding the two terms gives derivative $a+d\xi+[A,\xi]=a+d_A\xi$, which is the displayed formula.

On an overlap write $s_\beta=s_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$ for its smooth transition map $g_{\alpha\beta}:U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\to SU(N)$. Local representatives of an adjoint section $\xi$ and an adjoint group section $u$ are defined by $\xi(x)=[s_\alpha(x),\xi_\alpha(x)]$ and $u(x)=[s_\alpha(x),u_\alpha(x)]$. They obey the transition rules $\xi_\beta=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}}\xi_\alpha$ and $u_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}u_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$.

For each integer $k>d/2+1$, define $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ by completion of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms, using weak derivatives of their local coefficients. Define $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ as the corresponding completion of smooth group-bundle sections, represented locally by matrix-valued $H^{k+1}$ maps satisfying the stated transition rule. After localization by the partition of unity and extension by zero to the coordinate balls, the higher-order Sobolev embedding gives unique continuous representatives (indeed $C^1$); the group-valued representatives take values in the closed subgroup $SU(N)$ everywhere. This embedding is the point-evaluation convention used below. If $p\in P$ lies over $x$ and $p=s_\alpha(x)h$, define $u(p):=h^{-1}u_\alpha(x)h$. The transition rule makes this independent of the chosen local section, and $u(x)=[p,u(p)]$. In particular, if $p_m=s_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$, then $u(p_m)=h_{\alpha m}^{-1}u_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$ is the value in the $p_m$-trivialization. The map $\widetilde u:P\to P$ defined by $\widetilde u(p):=p\,u(p)$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$, with inverse $\widetilde{u^{-1}}$; it is smooth when $u$ is smooth. Conversely, if $\Phi:P\to P$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$ commuting with the right $SU(N)$ action, write $\Phi(p)=p\,g_p$ for the unique $g_p\in SU(N)$. Equivariance gives $g_{ph}=h^{-1}g_ph$, so $u(x):=[p,g_p]$ for $p\in P_x$ is a well-defined $C^1$ adjoint-group section. These assignments are inverse; in the smooth case they identify smooth sections with the smooth gauge group defined by principal-bundle automorphisms.

Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$, equivalently the sections whose associated bundle automorphism fixes $p_m$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology and multiplication $[u][v]=[uv]$, well-defined since $Z_N$ is central.

Specify its Hilbert Lie structure as follows, using the Hilbert Lie structure on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ established by the calculus lemma. Let $q:\mathcal G_{k+1}\to\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ be the coset projection. Since $Z_N$ is finite and the group is Hausdorff, choose an identity chart neighborhood $V$ with $V^{-1}V\cap Z_N=\{e\}$, by continuity of $(v,w)\mapsto v^{-1}w$ at $(e,e)$. The map $q$ is open because $q^{-1}(q(O))=\bigcup_{z\in Z_N}Oz$ for every open $O$. Consequently $q|_{uV}:uV\to q(uV)$ is a homeomorphism for each $u$, and transport the translated Hilbert charts through these maps. On an overlap, two lifts differ locally by multiplication by a fixed element of the discrete group $Z_N$, so chart changes are smooth. Distinct cosets have disjoint open neighborhoods: if $v^{-1}w\notin Z_N$, continuity and finiteness give neighborhoods $O_v,O_w$ with $O_v^{-1}O_w\cap Z_N=\varnothing$, and their images under $q$ are disjoint. Thus the quotient is Hausdorff. Its countable base descends from that of the Sobolev section space by the open map $q$. Multiplication and inversion are smooth in these charts because they lift locally to the corresponding smooth operations on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. This defines a Hilbert Lie group with the stated quotient topology, and $q$ is a local diffeomorphism.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty:=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ be the group of smooth adjoint-group sections under pointwise multiplication, identified above with the smooth gauge group. Give it the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. For a connection form $\omega$, write $A_\alpha=s_\alpha^*\omega$ for its local form. The right-principal convention gives $A_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}A_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$. The right gauge action is locally $A_\alpha^u:=u_\alpha^{-1}A_\alpha u_\alpha+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha$. For smooth $u$, this is the pullback by $\widetilde u$: for $X\in T_xM$, $d(\widetilde u\circ s_\alpha)_xX=d(R_{u_\alpha(x)})_{s_\alpha(x)}\,ds_\alpha(X)+(u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha(X))_P(s_\alpha(x)u_\alpha(x))$, and the connection equivariance and vertical reproduction identities give the displayed formula. For Sobolev $u$, the calculus lemma verifies that the local forms patch under the stated transition rules and define a smooth action on the Sobolev spaces above. For an adjoint section $\xi$, set $d_A\xi:=d\xi+[A,\xi]$ using the degree-one Lie-algebra-valued-form bracket. In local coordinates and an orthonormal adjoint frame, define the formal adjoint on an adjoint-valued one-form $a$ by $(d_A^*a)=-g^{ij}(\nabla_i^{\mathrm{LC}}a_j+[A_i,a_j])$, where $\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}$ differentiates the covector index. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

For $A\in\mathcal A_k$, parallel transport of its $C^1$ connection form around piecewise smooth loops based at $p_m$ defines a subgroup $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)\subseteq SU(N)$. Call $A$ irreducible when this subgroup leaves no nonzero proper complex subspace of $\mathbb C^N$ invariant; changing the chosen frame conjugates the subgroup and leaves this condition unchanged. Write $\mathcal A_k^*$ and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ for the irreducible loci. Once the calculus lemma verifies the group action, define orbit equivalence by $A\sim B$ exactly when $B=A^u$ for some gauge section $u$; all resulting quotients carry the quotient topology, whose open sets are those with open inverse image under the orbit projection.

Assume the configuration data of the preceding definition. For every integer $k>d/2+1$, all finite-atlas Sobolev norms on the specified section and form spaces are equivalent, and $H^k$ embeds continuously in $C^1$. Put $\mathcal M:=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$, where $SU(N)$ acts by matrix conjugation and $H^r(\mathcal M)$ uses the same finite-atlas completion for each integer $r\ge0$. Pointwise multiplication is a bounded bilinear map $H^k(\mathcal M)\times H^k(\mathcal M)\to H^k(\mathcal M)$; its restriction to adjoint Lie algebra sections has this matrix-bundle target, whereas the commutator is a bounded bilinear map $H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)\times H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)\to H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)$. The set $\mathcal G_{k+1}=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ is a Hilbert Lie group modeled on $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$, and the right gauge action $\mathcal A_k\times\mathcal G_{k+1}\to\mathcal A_k$ is smooth. At $(A,e)$ its differential, in the affine and exponential coordinates, is

$$D\bigl((A+a)^{\exp\xi}\bigr)_{(0,0)}(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi,$$

where $a\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $\xi\in H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be continuous on an open time-state-parameter domain and locally state-Lipschitz with one constant on compact cylinders. Near fixed data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$, the solutions supplied by Picard-Lindelof exist on one common compact time interval and depend jointly and uniformly continuously there on the initial time, initial state, and parameter. Quantitatively, if the common time interval has length at most $H$, $\|F\|_2\le M$, and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$, then solutions through $(t_0,x_0)$ and $(s,y_0)$ satisfy

$$\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2\le e^{LH}\bigl(\|x_0-y_0\|_2+M|s-t_0|+H\,\omega(\|\lambda-\mu\|_2)\bigr),$$

where $\omega(r)\to0$ is a uniform modulus for the parameter dependence of $F$ on that cylinder.

Let $J$ be a nonempty compact interval and $n\ge1$. Say that a sequence of continuous maps $x_m:J\to\mathbb R^n$ is uniformly bounded when one $M$ satisfies $\|x_m(t)\|_2\le M$ for all $m,t$, and equicontinuous when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|s-t|<\delta$ implies $\|x_m(s)-x_m(t)\|_2<\varepsilon$ for every $m$. Every such sequence has a subsequence that converges uniformly to a continuous map $x:J\to\mathbb R^n$. The construction requires no choice principle.

A uniformly bounded equicontinuous sequence of $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on a nonempty compact interval has a uniformly convergent subsequence.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary of real dimension $n\ge2$, equipped with a smooth positive density, and $E\to M$ a finite-rank real Euclidean or complex Hermitian smooth vector bundle. Let $P$ be a smooth-coefficient second-order differential operator on $E$, formally symmetric for the density and metric, whose positive-frequency principal symbol is
$$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a_x(\xi,\xi)I_{E_x},$$
where $a$ is a smooth positive-definite real quadratic form on cotangent vectors. Thus in any local frame $P=-a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+B^j\partial_j+C$, with scalar real positive-definite $a^{ij}$ and matrix-valued lower coefficients. Nonnegativity of $P$ is not needed here.

For nonnegative integers $k$, define $H^k(M,E)$ by requiring the coefficients of each member of a finite smooth partition of unity times the section, in precompact bundle charts and extended by zero, to lie in $H^k(\mathbb R^n)$; the norm is the square root of the sum of these component Sobolev norms squared. Different such choices give equivalent norms. The following hold.

1. These are Hilbert spaces, smooth sections are dense, $H^0=L^2$ with equivalent norms, $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ is compact, and $H^k\hookrightarrow C^r$ continuously whenever $k>r+n/2$.
2. If $u\in H^1$ and $Pu=f\in H^k$ distributionally, then $u\in H^{k+2}$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2}).$$
In particular smooth data give smooth weak solutions. The same estimate holds for all $u\in H^{k+2}$.
3. For sufficiently large real $\lambda>0$, $P+\lambda:H^2\to L^2$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse $B:L^2\to H^2$. As an operator on $L^2$, $B$ is compact, injective and selfadjoint, has dense range $H^2$, and the unbounded operator $P$ with domain exactly $H^2$ is selfadjoint. The map $B:H^k\to H^{k+2}$ is bounded for every nonnegative integer $k$ and preserves smooth sections.
4. It supplies two-sided parametrices **modulo compact operators**:
$$PB=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad BP=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }H^2.$$
Here on the second space $B$ denotes its restriction after inclusion $H^2\hookrightarrow L^2$; it is compact on $H^2$. No assertion concerning arbitrary-order elliptic operators, or pseudodifferential symbol classes, is part of this theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $\pi$ on a nonzero complex Hilbert space
$H$ and $\rho$ on a nonzero complex Hilbert space $K$ be irreducible strongly
continuous unitary representations of the same topological group $G$. Every
bounded self-intertwiner of $\pi$ is a scalar multiple of $I_H$. If a nonzero
bounded intertwiner $T:H\to K$ satisfies $T\pi(g)=\rho(g)T$ for every $g\in G$,
then $\pi$ and $\rho$ are unitarily equivalent. Consequently, inequivalent
irreducible representations have no nonzero bounded intertwiner.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the configuration data of the preceding definition. For every integer $k>d/2+1$, all finite-atlas Sobolev norms on the specified section and form spaces are equivalent, and $H^k$ embeds continuously in $C^1$. Put $\mathcal M:=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$, where $SU(N)$ acts by matrix conjugation and $H^r(\mathcal M)$ uses the same finite-atlas completion for each integer $r\ge0$. Pointwise multiplication is a bounded bilinear map $H^k(\mathcal M)\times H^k(\mathcal M)\to H^k(\mathcal M)$; its restriction to adjoint Lie algebra sections has this matrix-bundle target, whereas the commutator is a bounded bilinear map $H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)\times H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)\to H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)$. The set $\mathcal G_{k+1}=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ is a Hilbert Lie group modeled on $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$, and the right gauge action $\mathcal A_k\times\mathcal G_{k+1}\to\mathcal A_k$ is smooth. At $(A,e)$ its differential, in the affine and exponential coordinates, is

$$D\bigl((A+a)^{\exp\xi}\bigr)_{(0,0)}(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi,$$

where $a\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $\xi\in H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$.

derivations.claim: A gauge section $u$ stabilizes $A$ exactly when the local action formula gives $du=uA-Au$, that is, $d_Au=0$. This equation says that $u$ is parallel for the induced connection on $\operatorname{Ad}P$. Since $M$ is connected, parallel transport determines $u$ everywhere from its value at $p_m$, so evaluation is injective on the stabilizer. A parallel section's value commutes with transport around every based loop, hence lies in the holonomy centralizer.

Let $B_j=A_j^{u_j}$ and work in the fixed finite atlas. The local action formula gives $du_j=u_jB_j-A_ju_j$. Since $u_j$ is unitary, its pointwise matrix norm is bounded uniformly. The convergent sequences $A_j,B_j$ are bounded in $H^k$, so the equation gives a uniform $H^1$ bound on $u_j$. If a uniform $H^r$ bound holds for some $0\le r\le k$, [F6] bounds both products on the right in $H^r$; hence $du_j$ is bounded in $H^r$ and $u_j$ is bounded in $H^{r+1}$. Induction through $r=k$ gives a uniform $H^{k+1}$ bound.

Conversely, let $g\in SU(N)$ commute with every element of $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)$. Transport $g$ from $p_m$ along any path to a point $x$ and conjugate it by the path's parallel-transport matrix. Two paths give the same value because their concatenation has holonomy commuting with $g$. This defines a parallel section $u$ with $u(p_m)=g$. To verify its endpoint regularity, fix $x_0$ and a coordinate ball $V$ with a smooth bundle trivialization. Choose a fixed piecewise smooth path from $x_m$ to $x_0$, then join $x_0$ to each $x\in V$ by radial paths that depend smoothly on $(t,x)$. On each varying segment the transport matrix solves $U(t,x)=U_0-\int_0^t C(s,x)U(s,x)\,ds$, where $C(s,x)=A_{\gamma_x(s)}(\dot\gamma_x(s))$ is $C^1$ in $(s,x)$ because the local coefficients of $A$ are $C^1$. On a compact subball, for a coordinate direction $e_j$, the difference quotients $Q_h(t,x)=(U(t,x+he_j)-U(t,x))/h$ satisfy
$$Q_h(t,x)=-\int_0^t C(s,x+he_j)Q_h(s,x)\,ds-\int_0^t \frac{C(s,x+he_j)-C(s,x)}{h}U(s,x)\,ds.$$
The coefficients in this linear integral equation converge uniformly as $h\to0$ to $C$ and $\partial_{x_j}C$. The equation
$$V_j(t,x)=-\int_0^t\bigl(C(s,x)V_j(s,x)+\partial_{x_j}C(s,x)U(s,x)\bigr)\,ds$$
has a unique continuous solution by successive approximation for the corresponding linear ODE. Because $\|(C(s,x+he_j)-C(s,x))/h\|$ is uniformly bounded by $\|\partial_{x_j}C\|_\infty$, the equation for $Q_h$ first gives $q_h(t)\le b+L\int_0^t q_h(s)\,ds$ with one $b$ independent of $h$. Iterating $n$ times gives $q_h(t)\le b\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}(Lt)^q/q!+\sup_s q_h(s)(Lt)^n/n!$; for each $h$, $q_h$ is bounded on the compact interval, so letting $n\to\infty$ yields $q_h(t)\le be^{LT}$ uniformly in $h$. Subtracting the equation for $V_j$ from that for $Q_h$ gives $f_h(t)\le a_h+L\int_0^t f_h(s)\,ds$, where $f_h(t):=\|Q_h(t,x)-V_j(t,x)\|$ and $a_h:=T(\|C(\cdot,x+he_j)-C(\cdot,x)\|_\infty\|V_j\|_\infty+\|(C(\cdot,x+he_j)-C(\cdot,x))/h-\partial_{x_j}C\|_\infty\|U\|_\infty)\to0$ uniformly on the compact cylinder. Iterating this inequality $n$ times gives $f_h(t)\le a_h\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}(Lt)^q/q!+\sup_s f_h(s)(Lt)^n/n!$. The already established uniform bound on $Q_h$ bounds the remainder; letting $n\to\infty$ yields $f_h(t)\le a_he^{Lt}\to0$. Thus $Q_h\to V_j$ uniformly. The same difference estimate applied at nearby $x$, together with continuity of $C$, $\partial_{x_j}C$, and $U$, shows $V_j$ is continuous in $(t,x)$. Hence $U$ is $C^1$ in the endpoint. Concatenating finitely many fixed and varying segments and changing smooth bundle frames preserve this regularity, so the path-independent section has $C^1$ local representatives. Since $M$ is compact, these representatives lie in $H^1$ in the finite-atlas norms. If $u\in H^r$ for some $1\le r\le k$, then the right side of $du=uA-Au$ is in $H^r$ by [F6], so $du\in H^r$ and $u\in H^{r+1}$. Induction gives $u\in H^{k+1}$, so $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and stabilizes $A$. Thus evaluation has exactly the stated image.

By [F4], a subsequence converges strongly in $H^k$ to a section $u$. The $H^k\hookrightarrow C^0$ embedding preserves the pointwise $SU(N)$ equations and the bundle transition law, so $u$ is a group-bundle section. In the gauge equation, $A_j\to A$, $B_j\to B$, and $u_j\to u$ in $H^k$; because $H^k$ is an algebra, $u_jB_j-A_ju_j\to uB-Au$ in $H^k$. Thus $du_j$ converges in $H^k$ and the local coefficients converge in $H^{k+1}$. The limit satisfies $du=uB-Au$, equivalently $B=A^u$, and $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$.

On the standard $\mathbb C^N$, the holonomy matrices are unitary. If the representation is irreducible, [F5] makes every matrix commuting with the representation a scalar $\lambda I_N$. Membership in $SU(N)$ gives $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda^N=1$, hence its centralizer is $Z_N$. The stabilizer equality from steps 1.1 and 2.1 therefore gives full stabilizer $Z_N$ and trivial reduced stabilizer.

For each $1\le r<N$, represent an $r$-plane in $\mathbb C^N$ by its Hermitian orthogonal projection $Q$, so the Grassmannian is $\{Q:Q^*=Q,\ Q^2=Q,\ \operatorname{tr}Q=r\}$ in the finite-dimensional matrix space. Such projections have norm one. Regard any sequence of them as constant curves on $[0,1]$; [F3] gives a uniformly convergent subsequence, and the three defining equations pass to its limit. Thus each Grassmannian is compact. Suppose $A_j\to A$ and each $A_j$ is reducible. A subsequence has a fixed invariant dimension $r$, and by compactness another subsequence of invariant projections converges to $Q$. For a fixed based piecewise smooth loop $\gamma$, subdivide it into finitely many segments lying in bundle charts. On one segment, let $C_j(t)$ and $C(t)$ be the local matrix coefficients in the parallel-transport equations for $A_j$ and $A$. Since $H^k\hookrightarrow C^1$ by [F1], $A_j\to A$ in $H^k$ implies $C_j\to C$ uniformly. There is a common bound $\|C_j\|_\infty\le L$, and the transport matrices $U_j,U$ have norm one. Their integral equations, with the same initial matrix on the first segment, give for $W_j=U_j-U$ the inequality $\|W_j(t)\|\le T\delta_j+L\int_0^t\|W_j(s)\|\,ds$, where $T$ is the segment length and $\delta_j=\|C_j-C\|_\infty\to0$. Iterating as in step 2.1 yields $\sup_t\|W_j(t)\|\le T e^{LT}\delta_j\to0$. At each later segment the initial matrices already converge, and the same inequality adds their vanishing initial difference to the right side. Induction over the finite subdivision proves $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A_j,\gamma)\to\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A,\gamma)$. Since the holonomy matrices are unitary and preserve $\operatorname{ran}Q_j$, they commute with $Q_j$; passing to the limit shows that $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A,\gamma)$ commutes with $Q$ for every loop. Therefore $\operatorname{ran}Q$ is a nonzero proper invariant subspace and $A$ is reducible. The reducible locus is closed, so $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open.

The action map is continuous by the preceding Sobolev-calculus lemma. For a compact subset of $\mathcal A_k^*\times\mathcal A_k^*$, any sequence in its inverse image has a subsequence whose connection and transformed-connection coordinates converge in that compact set. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 give a further subsequence of gauge classes converging in $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$, while step 3.1 gives freeness. The inverse image is closed because the action map is continuous, so sequential compactness in these metrizable spaces is compactness. This proves properness. By step 3.1 the reduced action is free.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement inherits basepoint p_m, excluding an empty M. If the irreducible locus is empty, its reduced action has empty domain and its properness assertion is vacuous; the all-connection stabilizer and subsequence clauses still retain their stated domains.
The stabilizer equation is checked at the identity section in step 1.1. 1.1.

Step 3.1 reduces the stabilizer to the finite center Z_N for irreducible A, so the reduced stabilizer has exactly one element. The original stabilizer still has N central elements; freeness is asserted only after quotienting by Z_N.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 identify stabilizers for every A, including reducible connections with larger holonomy centralizer. Step 3.1 restricts the trivial reduced-stabilizer conclusion to irreducible A; it does not discard the center before that restriction.
Step 4.1 ranges over invariant dimensions 1<=r<N, excluding zero and the full N-plane from reducibility. The regularity threshold k>d/2+1 remains strict throughout the Sobolev action Statement.

A1 retains full AC. Step 4.1 extracts convergent subsequences of invariant projections via the stated compactness supplier, and steps 1.2 and 2.2 use Sobolev compactness. The proof does not claim a choice-free subsequence selection theorem.

For the stabilizer characterization, step 1.1 shows A^u=A implies d_Au=0 and that u(p_m) commutes with every holonomy matrix. Step 5.1 obtains compact-preimage properness from the convergent-sequence criterion in the stated metrizable spaces.

Step 2.1 constructs the unique parallel stabilizing section from every centralizing value in SU(N), proving the reverse centralizer correspondence. Conversely, compact-preimage properness on the reduced irreducible action supplies a subsequence over any convergent pair there; it does not characterize reducible stabilizers.

risk_review.notes: Checked all seven steps and F1-F6 independently. The multiplier estimate holds for every 0<=r<=k because residual orders sum to >d/2; unitary pointwise bounds start H1 induction. Rellich gives Hk convergence and the gauge equation upgrades it to H^{k+1}. Parallel centralizer extension is path independent; endpoint C1 regularity is proved by integral difference quotients, not attributed to a merely continuous ODE theorem. Schur applies to the nonzero finite-dimensional unitary defining module. Projection matrices of fixed rank form a compact set; loopwise convergence uses one fixed subsequence of projections for all loops. Metric sequential compactness establishes properness, including reducible inputs. Full AC and N=2 cases retained.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix an integer $N\ge2$. Write $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ for the complex $N\times N$ matrices, $U^*=\overline U^{\mathsf T}$ for conjugate transpose, and $I_N$ for the identity matrix. Define the special unitary matrix group

$$SU(N):=\{U\in\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C):U^*U=I_N,\ \det U=1\},$$

with matrix multiplication and the following real embedded smooth structure. Identify $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ with $\mathbb R^{2N^2}$ by the real and imaginary matrix entries, and let $\operatorname{Herm}_N=\{H:H^*=H\}$ have its induced real vector-space structure. Equip $U(N)=\{U:U^*U=I_N\}$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $I_N$ of the smooth map $F:\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)\to\operatorname{Herm}_N$, $F(U)=U^*U$, where $\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)=\{U:\det U\ne0\}$. Equip $S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ with its embedded circle structure and $SU(N)$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $1$ of $\det:U(N)\to S^1$. These are the embedded structures in the stated real matrix space. Its real Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{su}(N):=\{X\in\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C):X^*=-X,\ \operatorname{tr}X=0\}$ with bracket $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. The standard unitary representation is the map $\rho:SU(N)\to U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ defined by $\rho(U)v=Uv$, where $h(v,w)=\sum_{j=1}^N\overline{v_j}w_j$ and $U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ consists of the complex-linear maps preserving $h$. Conjugation is $\operatorname{Ad}_U z=UzU^{-1}$ for either $z\in SU(N)$ or $z\in\mathfrak{su}(N)$.

Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the representation $\rho$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.

Choose one finite smooth bundle atlas of local sections $(U_\alpha,s_\alpha)$ whose coordinate images are bounded balls, and a subordinate partition of unity with each cutoff compactly supported in its chart. On an overlap write $s_\beta=s_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$ for its smooth transition map $g_{\alpha\beta}:U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\to SU(N)$. Local representatives of an adjoint section $\xi$ and an adjoint group section $u$ are defined by $\xi(x)=[s_\alpha(x),\xi_\alpha(x)]$ and $u(x)=[s_\alpha(x),u_\alpha(x)]$. They obey the transition rules $\xi_\beta=\operatorname{Ad}_{g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}}\xi_\alpha$ and $u_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}u_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}$.

For each integer $k>d/2+1$, define $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ by completion of smooth sections in the resulting finite-atlas norms, using weak derivatives of their local coefficients. Define $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ as the corresponding completion of smooth group-bundle sections, represented locally by matrix-valued $H^{k+1}$ maps satisfying the stated transition rule. After localization by the partition of unity and extension by zero to the coordinate balls, the higher-order Sobolev embedding gives unique continuous representatives (indeed $C^1$); the group-valued representatives take values in the closed subgroup $SU(N)$ everywhere. This embedding is the point-evaluation convention used below. If $p\in P$ lies over $x$ and $p=s_\alpha(x)h$, define $u(p):=h^{-1}u_\alpha(x)h$. The transition rule makes this independent of the chosen local section, and $u(x)=[p,u(p)]$. In particular, if $p_m=s_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$, then $u(p_m)=h_{\alpha m}^{-1}u_\alpha(x_m)h_{\alpha m}$ is the value in the $p_m$-trivialization. The map $\widetilde u:P\to P$ defined by $\widetilde u(p):=p\,u(p)$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$, with inverse $\widetilde{u^{-1}}$; it is smooth when $u$ is smooth. Conversely, if $\Phi:P\to P$ is a $C^1$ bundle automorphism over $\operatorname{id}_M$ commuting with the right $SU(N)$ action, write $\Phi(p)=p\,g_p$ for the unique $g_p\in SU(N)$. Equivariance gives $g_{ph}=h^{-1}g_ph$, so $u(x):=[p,g_p]$ for $p\in P_x$ is a well-defined $C^1$ adjoint-group section. These assignments are inverse; in the smooth case they identify smooth sections with the smooth gauge group defined by principal-bundle automorphisms.

Define the affine configuration space $\mathcal A_k:=A_0+H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the set $\mathcal G_{k+1}:=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ of Sobolev gauge sections. Its based subset is $\mathcal G_{k+1,m}:=\{u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}:u(p_m)=e\}$, equivalently the sections whose associated bundle automorphism fixes $p_m$. Let $Z_N=\{zI_N:z^N=1\}$ be the center of $SU(N)$, viewed as constant gauge sections. Indeed, if $Z=(z_{ij})$ is central and $D=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in SU(N)$, then $(t_j-t_i)z_{ij}=0$. For each $i\ne j$ one can choose such a diagonal matrix with $t_i\ne t_j$, so $Z$ is diagonal. Commuting with the determinant-one unitary rotation whose block on the $(i,j)$ coordinates is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$ for $t\notin\pi\mathbb Z$ forces the $i$th and $j$th diagonal entries equal. Hence $Z=zI_N$; determinant one gives $z^N=1$, and conversely every such scalar is central. Write $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ for the set of $Z_N$-cosets with quotient topology and multiplication $[u][v]=[uv]$, well-defined since $Z_N$ is central.

Specify its Hilbert Lie structure as follows, using the Hilbert Lie structure on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ established by the calculus lemma. Let $q:\mathcal G_{k+1}\to\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ be the coset projection. Since $Z_N$ is finite and the group is Hausdorff, choose an identity chart neighborhood $V$ with $V^{-1}V\cap Z_N=\{e\}$, by continuity of $(v,w)\mapsto v^{-1}w$ at $(e,e)$. The map $q$ is open because $q^{-1}(q(O))=\bigcup_{z\in Z_N}Oz$ for every open $O$. Consequently $q|_{uV}:uV\to q(uV)$ is a homeomorphism for each $u$, and transport the translated Hilbert charts through these maps. On an overlap, two lifts differ locally by multiplication by a fixed element of the discrete group $Z_N$, so chart changes are smooth. Distinct cosets have disjoint open neighborhoods: if $v^{-1}w\notin Z_N$, continuity and finiteness give neighborhoods $O_v,O_w$ with $O_v^{-1}O_w\cap Z_N=\varnothing$, and their images under $q$ are disjoint. Thus the quotient is Hausdorff. Its countable base descends from that of the Sobolev section space by the open map $q$. Multiplication and inversion are smooth in these charts because they lift locally to the corresponding smooth operations on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. This defines a Hilbert Lie group with the stated quotient topology, and $q$ is a local diffeomorphism.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty:=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ be the group of smooth adjoint-group sections under pointwise multiplication, identified above with the smooth gauge group. Give it the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$. For a connection form $\omega$, write $A_\alpha=s_\alpha^*\omega$ for its local form. The right-principal convention gives $A_\beta=g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}A_\alpha g_{\alpha\beta}+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$. The right gauge action is locally $A_\alpha^u:=u_\alpha^{-1}A_\alpha u_\alpha+u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha$. For smooth $u$, this is the pullback by $\widetilde u$: for $X\in T_xM$, $d(\widetilde u\circ s_\alpha)_xX=d(R_{u_\alpha(x)})_{s_\alpha(x)}\,ds_\alpha(X)+(u_\alpha^{-1}du_\alpha(X))_P(s_\alpha(x)u_\alpha(x))$, and the connection equivariance and vertical reproduction identities give the displayed formula. For Sobolev $u$, the calculus lemma verifies that the local forms patch under the stated transition rules and define a smooth action on the Sobolev spaces above. For an adjoint section $\xi$, set $d_A\xi:=d\xi+[A,\xi]$ using the degree-one Lie-algebra-valued-form bracket. In local coordinates and an orthonormal adjoint frame, define the formal adjoint on an adjoint-valued one-form $a$ by $(d_A^*a)=-g^{ij}(\nabla_i^{\mathrm{LC}}a_j+[A_i,a_j])$, where $\nabla^{\mathrm{LC}}$ differentiates the covector index. This is the $L^2$ adjoint for the Riemannian volume and stated fiber metric; its local coefficient formula defines a distribution at Sobolev regularity.

For $A\in\mathcal A_k$, parallel transport of its $C^1$ connection form around piecewise smooth loops based at $p_m$ defines a subgroup $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)\subseteq SU(N)$. Call $A$ irreducible when this subgroup leaves no nonzero proper complex subspace of $\mathbb C^N$ invariant; changing the chosen frame conjugates the subgroup and leaves this condition unchanged. Write $\mathcal A_k^*$ and $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ for the irreducible loci. Once the calculus lemma verifies the group action, define orbit equivalence by $A\sim B$ exactly when $B=A^u$ for some gauge section $u$; all resulting quotients carry the quotient topology, whose open sets are those with open inverse image under the orbit projection.

Assume the configuration data and integer $k>d/2+1$ from the preceding definition, and let $\mathcal A_k^*$ be the locus where the holonomy representation on $\mathbb C^N$ is irreducible. For any $A\in\mathcal A_k$, evaluation at $p_m$ identifies its stabilizer in $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ with the centralizer of $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)$ in $SU(N)$. Thus an irreducible connection has stabilizer exactly $Z_N$, and the induced action of $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}=\mathcal G_{k+1}/Z_N$ on $\mathcal A_k^*$ is free. The subset $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open in $\mathcal A_k$.

The Sobolev action is proper: if $A_j\to A$ and $A_j^{u_j}\to B$ in $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ for sequences $A_j,A,B\in\mathcal A_k$ and $u_j\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$, then some subsequence $u_{j_\ell}$ converges in $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ to $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and $B=A^u$. Equivalently, the action map $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}\times\mathcal A_k^*\to\mathcal A_k^*\times\mathcal A_k^*$ is proper, meaning inverse images of compact sets are compact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. If additionally $(Pu,u)_2\ge0$ for smooth $u$, then $P$ and $G$ are nonnegative on their respective domains.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary of real dimension $n\ge2$, equipped with a smooth positive density, and $E\to M$ a finite-rank real Euclidean or complex Hermitian smooth vector bundle. Let $P$ be a smooth-coefficient second-order differential operator on $E$, formally symmetric for the density and metric, whose positive-frequency principal symbol is
$$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a_x(\xi,\xi)I_{E_x},$$
where $a$ is a smooth positive-definite real quadratic form on cotangent vectors. Thus in any local frame $P=-a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+B^j\partial_j+C$, with scalar real positive-definite $a^{ij}$ and matrix-valued lower coefficients. Nonnegativity of $P$ is not needed here.

For nonnegative integers $k$, define $H^k(M,E)$ by requiring the coefficients of each member of a finite smooth partition of unity times the section, in precompact bundle charts and extended by zero, to lie in $H^k(\mathbb R^n)$; the norm is the square root of the sum of these component Sobolev norms squared. Different such choices give equivalent norms. The following hold.

1. These are Hilbert spaces, smooth sections are dense, $H^0=L^2$ with equivalent norms, $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^k$ is compact, and $H^k\hookrightarrow C^r$ continuously whenever $k>r+n/2$.
2. If $u\in H^1$ and $Pu=f\in H^k$ distributionally, then $u\in H^{k+2}$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2}).$$
In particular smooth data give smooth weak solutions. The same estimate holds for all $u\in H^{k+2}$.
3. For sufficiently large real $\lambda>0$, $P+\lambda:H^2\to L^2$ is a bounded bijection with bounded inverse $B:L^2\to H^2$. As an operator on $L^2$, $B$ is compact, injective and selfadjoint, has dense range $H^2$, and the unbounded operator $P$ with domain exactly $H^2$ is selfadjoint. The map $B:H^k\to H^{k+2}$ is bounded for every nonnegative integer $k$ and preserves smooth sections.
4. It supplies two-sided parametrices **modulo compact operators**:
$$PB=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad BP=I-\lambda B\quad\hbox{on }H^2.$$
Here on the second space $B$ denotes its restriction after inclusion $H^2\hookrightarrow L^2$; it is compact on $H^2$. No assertion concerning arbitrary-order elliptic operators, or pseudodifferential symbol classes, is part of this theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $m\ge1$. For every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $C=C(n,m,\varepsilon)$ such that every
$u\in H^{m+1}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ satisfies
$$\|D^mu\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le\varepsilon\,\|D^{m+1}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}+C\,\|D^{m-1}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)},$$
and the same estimate holds for every $u\in H^{m+1}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ whose
class vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact subset of $\Omega$. In
both displays
$$\|D^ju\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n,\,|\alpha|=j}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 .$$
In particular, for $u\in H^2_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$,
$$\|Du\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le\varepsilon\|D^2u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}+C_\varepsilon\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)} .$$
The constants are not asserted sharp, and the estimate is the tool that
absorbs commutator terms linear in the highest derivatives.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach
spaces over the same scalar field, let $T:X\to Y$ be a Fredholm operator and let
$K:X\to Y$ be compact ([[def-fredholm-operator-cokernel-and-index]],
[[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T+K$
is Fredholm and $\operatorname{ind}(T+K)=\operatorname{ind}T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces over the same scalar field
([[def-banach-space]]).

1. If $R\in\mathcal B(X)$ satisfies $\|R\|<1$
   ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), then $I-R$ is
   invertible with inverse the operator-norm limit of the partial sums
   $\sum_{n<N}R^n$, the norm limit being taken in
   $\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]), and
   $$\Bigl\|\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R^n\Bigr\|\le\frac{1}{1-\|R\|}.$$
2. If $A\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is invertible with $A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$ and
   $E\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ satisfies $\|A^{-1}E\|<1$, then $A+E$ is invertible
   with $(A+E)^{-1}=\bigl(I+A^{-1}E\bigr)^{-1}A^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the configuration data of the preceding definition. For every integer $k>d/2+1$, all finite-atlas Sobolev norms on the specified section and form spaces are equivalent, and $H^k$ embeds continuously in $C^1$. Put $\mathcal M:=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$, where $SU(N)$ acts by matrix conjugation and $H^r(\mathcal M)$ uses the same finite-atlas completion for each integer $r\ge0$. Pointwise multiplication is a bounded bilinear map $H^k(\mathcal M)\times H^k(\mathcal M)\to H^k(\mathcal M)$; its restriction to adjoint Lie algebra sections has this matrix-bundle target, whereas the commutator is a bounded bilinear map $H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)\times H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)\to H^k(\operatorname{ad}P)$. The set $\mathcal G_{k+1}=H^{k+1}(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ is a Hilbert Lie group modeled on $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$, and the right gauge action $\mathcal A_k\times\mathcal G_{k+1}\to\mathcal A_k$ is smooth. At $(A,e)$ its differential, in the affine and exponential coordinates, is

$$D\bigl((A+a)^{\exp\xi}\bigr)_{(0,0)}(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi,$$

where $a\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$ and $\xi\in H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$.

The three terms in $K_A$ from step 1.1 satisfy $\|K_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}\le C_A\|\xi\|_{H^k}$. The Sobolev interpolation estimate $\|\xi\|_{H^k}\le\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}+C_\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{L^2}$ follows by finite-atlas localization and the estimate in [F5]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so that the resulting $H^{k+1}$ term is absorbed into the left side. This yields $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A'(\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$.

If $\Delta_A\xi=0$ for $\xi\in H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$, the formal-adjoint identity, first for smooth approximants and then by Sobolev continuity, gives $0=\langle\Delta_A\xi,\xi\rangle_{L^2}=\|d_A\xi\|_{L^2}^2$. Hence $d_A\xi=0$. Parallel transport makes $\xi$ determined by $\xi(p_m)$, and that value commutes with holonomy. By [F2], $\exp(t\xi(p_m))$ lies in the finite group $Z_N$ for every real $t$, because $\xi(p_m)$ commutes with holonomy. The path is continuous and equals the identity at $t=0$, so it is constant; differentiating at zero gives $\xi(p_m)=0$. Parallel transport then gives $\xi=0$.

Since $\Delta_A$ is Fredholm of index zero and its kernel is zero by step 3.1, its cokernel has dimension zero. Its range is closed by the Fredholm property, so $\Delta_A$ is onto and therefore bijective.

If no constant bounded $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}$ by $\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$, choose $\|\xi_j\|_{H^{k+1}}=1$ with $\Delta_A\xi_j\to0$. By [F4], a subsequence converges in $L^2$; applying the estimate of step 2.2 to differences shows it is Cauchy in $H^{k+1}$. Its limit has $H^{k+1}$ norm one and lies in $\ker\Delta_A$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A''\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$. Together with bijectivity this proves the inverse $G_A$ is bounded.

The operator-valued map $A\mapsto\Delta_A\in\mathcal B(H^{k+1},H^{k-1})$ is a continuous polynomial of degree at most two in the local coefficients of $A$, by step 1.1 and the product estimates [F8]. Near a fixed irreducible $A$, write $\Delta_{A+h}=\Delta_A+E(h)$; for small $h$, [F7] gives $(\Delta_{A+h})^{-1}=(I+G_AE(h))^{-1}G_A=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-G_AE(h))^nG_A$. On a neighborhood where $\|G_AE(h)\|\le\rho<1$, the Neumann series converges in operator norm. Its $m$-th derivative is bounded termwise by a constant times $n^m\rho^{n-m}$ for $n\ge m$, whose series converges; hence all derivatives converge uniformly on a smaller neighborhood. This proves that inversion and $A\mapsto G_A$ are smooth there.

Define $\Pi_A=d_AG_Ad_A^*$. The Sobolev orders give a bounded map $H^k(\Omega^1(\operatorname{ad}P))\to H^k(\Omega^1(\operatorname{ad}P))$. Since $\Delta_A G_A=I$ and $G_A\Delta_A=I$, one has $\Pi_A d_A\xi=d_A\xi$ and $d_A^*(I-\Pi_A)a=0$ for every $\xi\in H^{k+1}$ and $a\in H^k$. Thus $\Pi_A$ is a bounded projection with range $\operatorname{im}d_A$, while $I-\Pi_A$ has range $\ker d_A^*$. Their ranges intersect trivially: if $d_A\xi\in\ker d_A^*$, then $\Delta_A\xi=0$, so step 3.1 gives $\xi=0$. This proves the direct-sum decomposition and projection formula. Smooth dependence of $G_A$, $d_A$, and $d_A^*$ from step 5.1 makes $\Pi_A$ smooth in $A$.

boundaries.evidence: The covariant Green Statement fixes an irreducible A on the pointed nonempty compact base, so it does not assert existence when that locus is empty. Zero Sobolev sections are present and step 6.1 applies both projections to them.
The zero-kernel boundary is established for the rough Laplacian in step 3.1.

Step 6.1 proves Pi_A d_A xi=d_A xi, so Pi_A acts as the identity on its image, while I-Pi_A maps onto ker d_A^*. This includes eigenvalue one of the projection and no normalization denominator is introduced.

Step 3.1 eliminates the zero-mode kernel using irreducibility. Reducible A, where parallel adjoint sections may exist, is outside the inverse claim; the zero right-hand side for an admissible A has solution xi=0.

Step 1.1 requires k-1>d/2 for its multiplication estimate, following the strict Statement bound k>d/2+1. The threshold equality is not included; the Neumann neighborhood in step 5.1 requires norm strictly below one.

The covariant Green argument explicitly inherits full AC through A1 and its elliptic/Fredholm suppliers. Step 4.2 uses subsequence compactness in a contradiction argument; the inverse itself is uniquely determined by the operator.

boundaries.reason: The covariant Green lemma proves an inverse and a direct-sum projection for an already irreducible connection. It does not claim that invertibility of a chosen operator characterizes every irreducible holonomy representation.

The Coulomb projection formula is a consequence of the specified Green inverse. No reverse implication derives the global irreducibility assumption from an arbitrary splitting of a space of one-forms.
